motion: Carbon capture is essential to fighting climate change.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: What is your concrete plan for carbon that remains after every feasible reduction? If your answer is simply to tolerate it, how can that be enough to fight climate change responsibly?

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: I accept that residual carbon deserves attention, but the main danger is treating removal as permission to keep emitting. Climate action is strongest when prevention leads and capture remains optional.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Consider a facility that cannot yet change its chemical process but can capture its remaining carbon today. That immediate reduction protects climate progress, proving capture is essential where direct cuts stop.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Today we debate the motion, "Carbon capture is essential to fighting climate change." Mari supports it, and Hugh opposes it. Each debater gets thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire. Then each gets thirty-second closings. I will give a ten-second cue before each limit.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Carbon capture is essential because some emissions cannot be eliminated quickly, especially from heavy industry and existing pollution. It can remove carbon while cleaner systems grow, buying time without pretending it replaces them. Climate safety needs both sharp cuts and reliable removal. That is where my case begins, and I will explain why delay makes the challenge harder.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, Mari.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Carbon capture may help with a narrow leftover problem, but that does not make it essential to fighting climate change. Mari's bridge can become a detour, keeping polluting systems alive and weakening pressure to replace them. The central task is stopping emissions at their source. We already have direct choices: use less energy, build cleaner power, and change industrial practice. Removal should not define climate success.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds warning.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If capture is treated as essential, it can excuse delay and protect polluters. Climate action is stronger when it cuts emissions directly first. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that concludes round one. On to round two. Round two is where the debaters address one another in turn. This round runs two and a half minutes from the moment I finish. I will call ten seconds before the end.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If direct cuts leave unavoidable industrial emissions, what will remove that carbon at the necessary scale if you reject capture as essential? Please name a workable replacement, not merely another promise of future reductions.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I grant that some emissions are difficult to eliminate, but difficulty does not prove capture is essential. Better industrial design and reduced demand can shrink those emissions, so climate progress should center on prevention, not uncertain removal.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Imagine a factory that has cut every practical source but still releases process carbon. Capturing that remainder prevents pollution that efficiency alone cannot stop. That example proves capture is essential for a complete climate response.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: When a cleaner industrial process can eliminate the same emissions, capture is not the essential choice; direct prevention is cheaper, simpler, and less vulnerable to failure. Under that condition, capture should come second.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: That condition is too narrow, because many industries cannot yet eliminate process emissions through cleaner design alone. Capture handles what prevention misses, and calling it secondary does not make the remaining carbon disappear-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Some residual emissions may require removal, but climate policy as a whole should prioritize avoiding emissions before addressing leftovers. That broader order still allows limited capture without making it essential to climate action.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If capture is merely limited, how will you handle unavoidable emissions while waiting for alternatives that may take decades? Can your plan protect the climate from those emissions now, rather than later?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Technology choices also affect jobs, costs, and public trust, and communities need changes they can maintain. Those concerns matter, but they should not distract us from the motion: direct cuts can fight climate change without making capture essential.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A cement plant may reduce fuel pollution yet still release carbon from its raw materials. Capturing that process carbon preserves the needed product while cutting its climate harm. This proves capture fills a real gap.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your cement example shows capture can be useful, not essential. If society can use less cement, redesign buildings, or develop different materials, reducing demand avoids that pollution without relying on capture.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Those alternatives may reduce demand, but they cannot remove every unavoidable process emission from remaining construction. A useful option is not enough; capture is essential wherever direct prevention cannot reach the source.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, time. And now we move on to Round three. Round three will be closing statements by each debater in turn. Here making her closing statement in support of the motion, Mari.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The strongest point is the gap between cutting emissions and removing what cuts cannot reach. Cleaner power and efficiency are vital, but they do not erase process emissions already produced or carbon already in the atmosphere. Capture gives us a way to address those leftovers while transformation continues. That makes it an essential part of serious climate action, not a substitute for it.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: We need both prevention and removal, because climate protection cannot leave unavoidable carbon unanswered. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Hugh? Do you want to try this one on?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Mari shows that capture may help in difficult cases, but she has not shown it is essential to fighting climate change. Essential means the effort cannot succeed without it. We can reduce demand, redesign production, and replace polluting systems directly. Those steps attack the cause rather than preserving it. Capture belongs only where other solutions fail, so climate action does not depend on it.
